What is going on: most of the Q3 pipeline growth is not real. On 29 Sept, 212 partner-tagged records ($6.2M) were bulk-loaded under Jun Okafor's account from a file that arrived in a team chat with the note "load before snapshot." None had any logged activity, and 171 of them duplicate 2024 closed-lost deals with dates moved into Q4. Rep-created deals convert at a steady 25%, the same as earlier this year, so the four reps are not failing to close. The webinar did not drive the surge.

How sure: high that the import is the main cause and that the reps' conversion is normal. Less sure who prepared and requested the file. Dana Wexley denies it, and the chat messages are gone.

Next steps: Do not sign the performance plans or release the requisitions. Restate coverage using rep-created deals only (about 1.9x, below the 3.0x gate). Quarantine the 212 records. Preserve the source file and import job record, and interview Okafor and channel members about who posted the file.

The pipeline jump is not real buying activity, and the reps did not get worse at closing. The Brightwell partner portal shows only 3 registered deals worth $0.21M, and Brightwell sent no bulk list. Reps' own opportunities held steady: win rate about 24% each quarter, and the four named reps are within the normal range. The webinars produced 11 opportunities worth $0.46M. The $5.9M "influenced" figure is mostly the imported records. Rep-created pipeline gives about 1.9x coverage, below the 3.0x gate. I don't know who prepared the file. Wexley's 28 Sept email asked for deals to be logged but did not mention a bulk import, and she denies supplying a file. That is unproven either way. Next steps: don't start performance plans and don't release the requisitions. Quarantine the imported records and restate coverage. Preserve and examine the import file's metadata, the import job record and the chat channel. Interview Okafor and the channel members before blaming anyone. Hold off on the webinar expansion.

The 26-point gap on the dashboard mostly reflects who joined Bridge Hours, not what the tutoring did. Participants were already much weaker in September: 91% scored below the 40th percentile, against 12% of non-participants. When the research office compared students with similar fall scores, the winter results were nearly identical. Participants gained slightly more in one band and slightly less in another, and the design cannot detect a small effect either way. I am fairly confident the raw gap is not evidence that the program lowers scores. I am not confident the program helps, and the Stepwise fraction methods that teachers flagged are unchecked.
Next steps: do not vote to end or expand on this data. Ask the research office for the comparison of students just either side of the 196 cut, promised by 27 Feb, and present that to the board in place of the raw chart. Have the math coordinator review Stepwise fraction lessons and observe sessions. Keep the referral list for now so the comparison stays valid.

The 26-point gap mostly reflects who gets into Bridge Hours, not what the program does. State rules require the district to offer intervention to every student below the 40th percentile in the fall, so 91% of participants started below that line. Their fall average was 182.8, against 215.1 for everyone else. Once students are compared with others who had similar fall scores, the gap nearly disappears. Participants' growth matches that of similar non-participants (+18.1 vs +17.2, +14.0 vs +14.2, +10.9 vs +10.2). Northgate's "faster growth" claim is also misleading, because low scorers gain more regardless of tutoring. So the evidence neither shows harm nor shows benefit. This comparison can't detect a small effect either way. I'm fairly confident (about 85%) that the dashboard doesn't show the program hurting students. I'm much less sure the program works. Next steps: (1) Show the board the like-for-like comparison instead of the raw chart. (2) Have the research office finish the comparison of students just either side of the 196 cutoff, due 27 Feb, and link attendance to scores. (3) Have the math coordinator check the teacher's report that Stepwise fraction methods conflict with classroom methods. (4) Don't cut or expand the contract yet. Don't drop the referral list, since it satisfies the state rule and would bias comparisons.

The rise in missed appointments at Corrie Lane is real and is not explained by the bus cut, staff behaviour, or recording errors. Eastgate, on the same bus route and with a similar patient mix, stayed flat at about 8%. Corrie Lane's own rate was about 8% a year earlier. Front-desk day-before calls are steady (about 91% of listed patients still called, versus 93% before). Miscoding explains only about half a point of the 13.4%. The most likely driver is the Tidewell configuration: the reminder moved from 48 hours to 7 days before, and booking lead times rose from about 19 to about 50 days. I cannot yet tell which of these two changes matters more, because the data cannot link booking lead time or reminder timing to individual outcomes. I am fairly confident about what is not the cause, and less sure about the mechanism. Next steps: run the planned 8-week split test of the reminder offset and get the vendor's appointment-level extract. Do not discipline front-desk staff, stop reporting the DNA rate, or change everything at once before the test. Confidence in the mechanism is moderate.

Next step: run the 8-week randomised test. Put the 48-hour reminder on half the templates, and ask the vendor for the appointment-level extract. Don't change the whole clinic's configuration yet. Keep reporting the DNA rate to the board, with a note that March and April are withheld.

What is going on: the slowdown is concentrated in one step. Claims worth $2,500–$10,000 now wait about 16 days for approval, up from under 1 day before April. Since the April change to the authority matrix, these approvals route to three team leads. Their tray grew from about 38 items a week to about 212, and the tray depth is now about 455. Investigation, imaging and the other stages barely moved. The hail surge has ended, the two departures did not slow investigation, and Quillfast processes documents faster than the old provider. The complaint rise is partly a logging change, not just slower claims.

How sure: moderately. The bottleneck pattern is strong. The complaint trend is not measurable like-for-like, and I did not check the $2,500 overpayment question.

What to do next: add interim approval capacity for the $2,500–$10,000 band, using experienced staff as second approvers with Internal Audit involved, and track approval wait weekly. Do not restore the $10,000 limit without audit sign-off, and do not penalise team leads. Defer any permanent authority decision and any return to the old imaging provider until the approval data supports them.

Turnaround doubled mainly because of the 1 April change to settlement authority. Adjusters' limit was cut from $10,000 to $2,500 after an audit found overpayments. Claims of $2,500–$10,000 (about 53% of closures) now need a team-lead approval. Those claims wait about 16 days for sign-off, up from 0.7. Their total time rose from 10.4 to 26 days. Other stages are almost unchanged, including investigation and document indexing, and claims under $2,500 and over $10,000 are unchanged. The three team leads went from about 38 to over 200 items a week. They approve about 199 a week, and the backlog keeps growing, from 11 to 455. The change record shows no workload assessment was done. The hail surge, the loss of two senior adjusters and the Quillfast switch don't explain the pattern. New claims and staffing were back to normal by June. Contract adjusters and a return to the old imaging provider would not fix the bottleneck. Don't sign either yet. Don't discipline the team leads. Don't drop the control unilaterally. Work with Internal Audit to add approval capacity for that band, for example by certifying senior adjusters as second approvers. Keep a second review on every claim in the band. Track time pending approval weekly. Wait for the December re-test before setting permanent thresholds. Whether the control actually reduces overpayments is still unmeasured. I'm confident in the main finding.

The payment failures are not caused by the v4.12 code. Since 3 March, a new reporting job (settle-recon, moved to a 15-minute daytime schedule on the shared Quillmark credential) fires bursts of search calls that push the credential over its 300-per-minute limit. Quillmark then returns HTTP 429 responses, and checkout shows them to customers as "card declined." Failures cluster in the first few minutes of each quarter hour. The canary (CHG-2231) is decisive: v4.11 pods failed at the same rate as v4.12 pods, so rolling back would not fix anything and would also undo the card-number masking required by SEC-2291 (deadline 13 March). I am fairly confident in this, though not certain; the bank-side evidence and the revenue link are not fully checked. Next steps: pause or revert settle-recon's daytime runs now and watch the 429 and failure rates; give that job its own credential; do not roll back v4.12. Do not tell the board that the failures caused the 9% revenue fall. Part of that drop coincides with the end of Winter Clearance, so the revenue figure needs separate analysis before any forecast restatement.

The failures are not caused by release v4.12. They come from Finance's settle-recon job, which has run every 15 minutes from 09:00 to 21:00 since 3 March (FIN-CHG-0187). It shares a gateway credential with checkout. Each run sends 360–430 search calls a minute, and the credential's limit is 300 a minute across all calls. Quillmark then returns 429 errors to checkout payments in those minutes. The v4.12 error handling shows all of these as "card declined".

The evidence for this is strong:
- 93% of failures fall in the first minutes of each quarter hour.
- Failures began at 09:00, before the 10:40 deploy.
- Failures stopped during the finance maintenance window on 6 March.
- Half the pods were rolled back to v4.11 in a test, and they failed at the same rate. 341 of their 351 failures were 429s.

Next steps:
1. Revert settle-recon to nightly, or pause its daytime runs. Then confirm the 429 rate and payment failures fall.
2. Don't roll back v4.12. A rollback wouldn't fix the failures and would reintroduce the SEC-2291 card-number logging problem.
3. Give settle-recon its own credential before any daytime schedule returns.
4. Fix the error mapping so 429s aren't shown as declines.
5. Don't attribute the 9% revenue drop to the failures yet. Conversion and order value also fell, the promotion changed traffic mix, and a roughly 3% failure rate can't explain 9% on its own. Measure the real lost revenue from failed attempts that were never retried successfully.

The overtime rise is mostly call-back pay for nightly closing, not vacancies or heat. Since the Kestrel closing contract lapsed on 31 March, maintenance staff have been paid call-backs to lock 41 Riverside, Eastgate and Millbrook sites; Summit Hill, which kept its contract, shows no spike. The Internal Audit review also found the claims by the two flagged employees matched lock logs, so the hotline allegation is not supported. Regular overtime barely moved, so the freeze explains little of the step change. Confidence is good on the closing link, moderate on the rest. The Eastgate favoritism claim is unproven. Next steps: restore contracted closing (or an equivalent) for the 41 sites and track call-back spending. Do not impose a blanket overtime cap or discipline the two employees, since that would leave gates and restrooms unlocked. Review the 3-hour minimum for short closing rounds. Fill vacancies on their own merits. Check Eastgate call-back assignment fairly. Workers' compensation claims cannot yet be tied to overtime, because hours worked were not recorded.

The overtime overrun comes mainly from the closing contract ending, not from the hiring freeze. Call-back pay rose from $38k to $289k. 1,962 of the 2,295 call-backs carry the CLOSE task code, and all are dated 1 April or later. None are in Summit Hill, whose closing contract continued. The three districts that lost the contract account for nearly all the increase. Summit Hill has 5 vacancies and its overtime was nearly flat. Eastgate has only 1 vacancy and its overtime nearly doubled. Holdover overtime grew only 1.5% in hours, so vacancies and heat explain little. The vacancy-versus-overtime correlation is mostly a coincidence of timing. Both rose in April. Internal Audit checked the fraud allegation against lock logs and found no padding, so don't discipline R-14 and R-22. Each 30–45 minute closing round is paid as three hours under the call-back minimum. That makes in-house closing far more costly than the $96k contract. I'm fairly confident, and I'd restore contracted closing now and track call-back spending. Don't impose an overtime cap, because members say they would stop taking call-backs and the sites wouldn't get locked. Keep the Eastgate favoritism concern open: sign-up sheets are being thrown away, so keep them from now on and review the assignment pattern before acting on the supervisor. The injury link to overtime is unproven, because claims aren't matched to hours worked. Match them to payroll. Don't pursue the eleven-position exemption as the fix.

Call-back pay rose from $38k to $289k. About 1,960 of the call-backs are closing duties that began on 1 April, the day the $96,000 night-closing contract lapsed. Summit Hill, which kept its contractor, saw almost no rise. Each 30–45 minute closing round is paid as three hours, so the contract's $96k saving cost far more in overtime. I'm about 85% sure of this.
The fraud allegation against two Riverside workers was checked against lock logs and not supported. Disciplining them would be wrong. The weather doesn't look like a main driver. The Eastgate favoritism complaint is plausible, since the same five or six people sign up and the sheets were discarded, but it isn't proven. The injury link to overtime is plausible but untested.
Next steps: restore contracted closing, or re-tender it, at the 41 sites. Track call-back spending against the April–September level. Keep and review Eastgate sign-up sheets and rotate assignments. Match injury claims to payroll hours. Don't impose an overtime cap, because closing is required for liability coverage. Don't take disciplinary action yet. Present the hiring exemption separately, on its own merits.

The 22 October overrun was caused by a manual backfill, not by platform trouble or extra load. Finance's Q3 restatement script (run by D. Varga, scheduled via at(1)) started at 00:58 and held an exclusive lock on stage_orders until 04:18. The nightly merge waited over two hours for that lock. Once it got the lock, the merge and mart builds ran at normal speed, so the run finished about an hour late. The Corvane incident ended at 03:37, before the lock was released, and order volume and the customer_ltv model were normal, so none of those explain the overrun. How sure I am: fairly high that the lock is the cause. Less sure whether the 1:00 start was a mistake for 13:00; the records don't settle what was intended.

Next steps: do not remove customer_ltv, switch off the banner, or discipline anyone on this evidence. Those would hide information or break retention calls without fixing the cause. Instead, require the nightly job owner to review any change that writes to tables the job uses, and add an alert for lock waits over 15 minutes. Ask the change board to confirm the intended start time for the restatement. Reschedule the restatement for a safe window, and have finance and the nightly owner agree on it.

The 22 Oct miss was caused by the Q3 margin restatement backfill, not by platform trouble or customer_ltv. The backfill started at 00:58 and held an exclusive lock on stage_orders until 04:18. The nightly merge waited 2h13m for it. The rest of the run took its normal time, and the lock wait alone explains the roughly one-hour overrun. The Corvane incident (02:52–03:37) fell inside the wait, and the log shows no slowdown from it. customer_ltv adds only about 19 minutes, and data volume was normal, so a tier upgrade or removing customer_ltv would not fix this. Removing customer_ltv would also hurt the retention team's 08:00 call list. Keep the banner: it stopped Finance from publishing stale numbers as current. Recommended action: make the job owner a required reviewer for changes touching its tables, bar writes to those tables from 01:00 to 06:00 without owner sign-off, and alert on lock waits over 15 minutes. Don't discipline D. Varga yet. The change was approved for 13:00–17:00, but why it ran at 01:00 is unconfirmed. The '1:00' note could be a misreading of 13:00, or a deliberate choice, and the repository history doesn't say. The review process also never listed the job owner. Ask Varga when they return from leave. I'm confident about the main cause and less sure about the reason for the start time.

The change checklist never involved the nightly job's owner, and no alert watches for lock waits. Recommended: add the nightly job's owner as a required reviewer for changes to its tables, restrict writes in the 01:00–06:00 window, and alert on lock waits over 15 minutes. Keep the banner, since Finance used it correctly. Don't move to a higher tier, and don't pull customer_ltv. Don't discipline anyone until you've heard from the implementer. Confidence is high on the cause and lower on the intent.
